questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.1 Identify AED purpose, shockable rhythms, and early defibrillation value
questions.text: What is the main purpose of an AED during cardiac arrest?

answers.text: To analyze the heart rhythm and deliver a shock when a shockable rhythm is detected
To replace chest compressions for the entire resuscitation
To give rescue breaths automatically
To confirm the person's identity before care begins

explanations.a: An AED identifies rhythms that may need defibrillation and can deliver a shock when indicated. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: AED use does not replace high-quality CPR.
explanations.c: AEDs do not ventilate the person.
explanations.d: AEDs are used for rhythm analysis and shocks, not identity verification.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.1 Identify AED purpose, shockable rhythms, and early defibrillation value
questions.text: What does defibrillation do?

answers.text: It checks the carotid pulse for the rescuer
Delivers a controlled electrical shock to interrupt an abnormal rhythm
It performs chest compressions automatically in all models
It gives oxygen through the lungs

explanations.a: The rescuer checks pulse; the AED analyzes rhythm.
explanations.b: Defibrillation uses a controlled shock to interrupt certain life-threatening abnormal rhythms. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Standard AEDs do not perform compressions.
explanations.d: Ventilation gives oxygen; defibrillation delivers electrical therapy.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.1 Identify AED purpose, shockable rhythms, and early defibrillation value
questions.text: During AED skills practice, which rhythms are shockable in basic AED teaching?

answers.text: A definite pulse with normal breathing
Normal sinus rhythm with normal breathing
Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Agonal gasps without rhythm analysis

explanations.a: A person with a definite pulse and normal breathing does not need defibrillation.
explanations.b: A normal rhythm with normal breathing is not a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm.
explanations.c: AEDs may advise a shock for shockable rhythms such as ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: Gasping alone does not determine whether a shock is needed.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.1 Identify AED purpose, shockable rhythms, and early defibrillation value
questions.text: Why is early defibrillation important?

answers.text: It eliminates the need to call for emergency help
It allows rescuers to stop CPR permanently after the first shock
It works best when delayed until the person wakes up
It improves survival chances when a shockable rhythm is present

explanations.a: AED use does not replace emergency response activation.
explanations.b: CPR usually resumes immediately after a shock.
explanations.c: Defibrillation should not be delayed when cardiac arrest is suspected.
explanations.d: Early AED use improves the chance of survival for shockable cardiac arrest rhythms. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.1 Identify AED purpose, shockable rhythms, and early defibrillation value
questions.text: According to AHA Part 3, what does an AED do that compressions alone cannot?

answers.text: Restart a normal rhythm by delivering a shock to interrupt VF or pulseless VT and let the heart's natural pacemaker resume coordinated activity
Pump blood through the body during arrest
Open the airway
Replace the need for any rescue breaths

explanations.a: AHA Part 3: AED defibrillation interrupts disorganized rhythms (VF/pulseless VT), allowing the natural pacemaker to resume — this complements but does not replace compressions.
explanations.b: Compressions pump blood; AEDs do not pump blood.
explanations.c: AEDs do not affect the airway.
explanations.d: Ventilations remain part of CPR; AEDs do not replace them.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.1 Identify AED purpose, shockable rhythms, and early defibrillation value
questions.text: Which two cardiac rhythms can an AED treat with a shock? (per AHA Part 3)

answers.text: Asystole and pulseless electrical activity
Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT)
Atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardia
Sinus rhythm and bradycardia

explanations.a: Asystole and PEA are non-shockable rhythms; AEDs will not deliver a shock for these.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3: VF and pVT are the two shockable rhythms targeted by AED defibrillation.
explanations.c: AF and SVT may be perfusing rhythms and are not AED targets.
explanations.d: Sinus rhythm and bradycardia are perfusing or near-perfusing; not AED targets.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.1 Identify AED purpose, shockable rhythms, and early defibrillation value
questions.text: AHA evidence shows that survival from VF cardiac arrest decreases by approximately what amount for every minute of delay in defibrillation if no CPR is provided?

answers.text: 1% per minute
2–3% per minute
4–5% per minute
7–10% per minute — early CPR slows this decline; early defibrillation is the most powerful single intervention for shockable arrest

explanations.a: 1%/min understates the importance of time-to-shock.
explanations.b: 2–3%/min is too low.
explanations.c: 4–5%/min is closer but still understated.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3: VF survival declines by approximately 7–10% for each minute without CPR or defibrillation; bystander CPR significantly slows this decline.

explanations.b: Trained rescuers help, but the underlying lever is time-to-shock.
explanations.c: Parking lot distance is not a meaningful AED placement metric; placement should focus on areas of population concentration.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3: time-to-defibrillation is the modifiable factor with the largest survival benefit; AED programs aim to reduce it.

answers.text: Power on → attach pads → analyze rhythm → deliver shock if advised
Attach pads → power on → deliver shock → analyze
Analyze → power on → deliver shock → attach pads
Deliver shock → power on → attach pads → analyze

explanations.a: AHA Part 3: power on first (this gives prompts), attach pads to bare chest, allow rhythm analysis, deliver shock if advised — universal across AED models.
explanations.b: Pad-before-power means the AED is not yet active to detect pad placement.
explanations.c: Analyze must follow pad attachment; pads are needed to read the rhythm.
explanations.d: Shock cannot be delivered before pads are attached and rhythm analyzed.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.2 Apply AED setup, pad placement, and universal operating steps
questions.keyword: AED pad placement anterior lateral upper right lower left
questions.text: According to AHA Part 3, where should AED pads be placed on an adult?

answers.text: Both pads on the front of the chest, side by side
One pad on the upper right chest just below the clavicle, the other on the lower left chest below the armpit (anterior-lateral) — or anterior-posterior on small chests when pads might overlap
Both pads on the back over the spine
Both pads over the abdomen

explanations.a: Side-by-side anterior placement does not allow current to traverse the heart effectively.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3: anterior-lateral placement (upper right + lower left) is the standard adult placement; anterior-posterior is used when pads might touch on small chests.
explanations.c: Posterior placement alone does not allow vector current through the heart.
explanations.d: Abdominal placement does not target the heart.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.2 Apply AED setup, pad placement, and universal operating steps
questions.keyword: chest hair AED razor pad adhesion
questions.text: A rescuer applies AED pads to an adult, but the patient has copious chest hair that prevents adhesion. According to AHA Part 3, what is the appropriate action?

answers.text: Apply the pads firmly anyway and hope they stick
Quickly remove the chest hair with the AED kit's razor (or by pulling pads down quickly to "wax" the area, then applying new pads); apply replacement pads firmly to bare skin
Skip the AED entirely
Wait for the hair to be shaved at the hospital before any AED use

explanations.a: Loose pads cause arcing, burns, and ineffective shock delivery.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3: most AED kits include a razor; quickly shave or "wax" the contact areas, then apply pads firmly to bare skin for full conductivity.
explanations.c: Skipping defibrillation costs lives.
explanations.d: Waiting for hospital care defeats the purpose of public-access defibrillation.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.3 Apply AED rhythm analysis, shock safety, and post-shock CPR actions
questions.text: During AED rhythm analysis, what should rescuers do?

answers.text: Stop CPR completely, ensure no one is touching the patient, and announce "Clear" — even small movements can confuse the AED's rhythm-analysis algorithm
Continue compressions to maintain perfusion
Hold the patient's hand for support
Connect a separate ECG to verify the AED

explanations.a: AHA Part 3: rhythm analysis requires no patient contact; movement (including compressions) interferes with the algorithm.
explanations.b: Continuing compressions during analysis introduces artifact and prevents accurate rhythm interpretation.
explanations.c: Touching the patient during analysis causes errors.
explanations.d: Lay rescuers do not connect external ECGs; the AED handles rhythm interpretation.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.3 Apply AED rhythm analysis, shock safety, and post-shock CPR actions
questions.keyword: no shock advised resume CPR 2 minutes
questions.text: After the AED prompts "no shock advised," what should the rescuers do?

answers.text: Wait for the AED to re-analyze before doing anything
Stop CPR for several minutes to recheck
Remove the AED pads (per AHA technique)
Resume CPR immediately starting with compressions for 2 minutes; the AED will re-analyze automatically at the end of the cycle

explanations.a: Waiting wastes critical perfusion time.
explanations.b: Multi-minute pauses lower coronary perfusion pressure dramatically.
explanations.c: Pads stay on for continued cycles of analysis.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3: "no shock advised" → resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes; pads stay on; the AED reanalyzes at the next cycle.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.3 Apply AED rhythm analysis, shock safety, and post-shock CPR actions
questions.keyword: after shock resume CPR no pulse check
questions.text: After delivering an AED shock, what is the correct action regarding pulse and CPR?

answers.text: Check carotid pulse for at least 1 minute before resuming any care
Resume CPR IMMEDIATELY starting with compressions; do NOT pause to check a pulse — pulse checks waste critical seconds and the AED will reanalyze in 2 minutes
Stop and observe the AED for color changes
Wait for the patient to wake up before resuming

explanations.a: Long pulse checks delay perfusion and contradict AHA guidance to minimize interruptions.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3 (2020 update): immediately resume compressions after a shock — do not pause to check a pulse; the AED will analyze again at the next 2-minute cycle.
explanations.c: AEDs do not have color-change indicators that warrant a pause.
explanations.d: Many ROSC patients do not "wake up"; waiting causes harm.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.3 Apply AED rhythm analysis, shock safety, and post-shock CPR actions
questions.text: During AED rhythm analysis on a patient in a moving ambulance, what is the recommended modification?

answers.text: Continue motion; the AED can compensate
Use double-strength shocks to overcome motion artifact
Skip rhythm analysis entirely
Bring the vehicle to a brief, complete stop during AED analysis to prevent motion artifact from corrupting the rhythm interpretation; resume motion once analysis is complete

explanations.a: Vehicle motion creates artifact that AEDs cannot reliably filter.
explanations.b: AED energy levels are pre-programmed; rescuers cannot increase them.
explanations.c: Rhythm analysis is essential; skipping it leads to inappropriate shocks or missed shockable rhythms.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3 / EMS guidance: stop the vehicle briefly during AED analysis to prevent artifact; resume motion afterward.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.3 Apply AED rhythm analysis, shock safety, and post-shock CPR actions
questions.keyword: metal bedframe conductive AED shock safety
questions.text: During AED use, the device prompts "shock advised" but the rescuer notices the patient is still in contact with a metal bedframe. What should be done?

answers.text: Deliver the shock anyway because shock is time-critical
Hold the patient's hand and deliver the shock to ground the energy
Remove the AED entirely and continue CPR only

Briefly move the patient away from the conductive contact (or insulate it), confirm "Clear" with no rescuer contact, and then deliver the shock — conductive contact creates a path for current to nearby people

explanations.a: Shock with conductive contact endangers rescuers and bystanders.
explanations.b: Holding the patient's hand routes current through the rescuer.
explanations.c: Removing the AED defeats the purpose of defibrillation.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3: insulate or remove conductive contact, confirm clear, then shock — protects rescuers from inadvertent shock through shared conductive surfaces.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.4 Recognize AED pad, skin, clothing, jewelry, hair, water, and medication patch considerations
questions.keyword: wet chest dry quickly AED pads
questions.text: When using an AED on a patient who is wet (drowning, sweat-soaked, etc.), what should the rescuer do?

answers.text: Apply pads while the chest is wet; AEDs work fine through water
Quickly dry the chest, then apply the pads firmly to bare skin — water on the chest can shunt current along the surface and reduce effective shock delivery
Wait for the patient to fully air-dry
Cover the chest with a towel and place pads on top

explanations.a: Wet skin reduces pad-skin contact and shunts current along the surface.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3: dry the chest quickly with a towel before applying pads, then apply firmly for good contact.
explanations.c: Air-drying takes too long during arrest.
explanations.d: A towel beneath pads insulates the pads from skin and prevents effective shock.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.4 Recognize AED pad, skin, clothing, jewelry, hair, water, and medication patch considerations
questions.keyword: medication patch remove wipe AED pad
questions.text: A patient wearing a transdermal medication patch (e.g., nitroglycerin, fentanyl) is in arrest. According to AHA Part 3, what should be done?

answers.text: Place the AED pad directly over the patch (per AHA technique)
Remove the medication patch and wipe the area clean before placing the AED pad — placing a pad over a patch causes burns and reduces shock efficacy
Cover the patch with extra gel before pad placement
Skip the AED if any patch is present

explanations.a: Pads over patches cause arcing burns at the patch site.
explanations.b: AHA Part 3: remove medication patches and wipe the area before pad placement to prevent burns and ensure effective shock delivery.
explanations.c: Adding gel does not solve the underlying conductivity issue.
explanations.d: Patch presence is not a contraindication to AED use; just remove the patch first.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.4 Recognize AED pad, skin, clothing, jewelry, hair, water, and medication patch considerations
questions.keyword: jewelry leave in place outside pad zone
questions.text: A patient in arrest is wearing a metal necklace and large earrings. According to AHA Part 3, what should the rescuer do?

answers.text: Leave the jewelry in place if it does not interfere with pad placement; only remove jewelry that is in the immediate pad-placement zone or could conduct current to nearby pads
Remove all jewelry from the patient's body
Cover all jewelry with bandages
Skip the AED until jewelry is removed

explanations.a: AHA Part 3: jewelry not in the pad zone does not interfere with shock delivery; only remove what could conduct current near pads.
explanations.b: Removing all jewelry wastes time during arrest.
explanations.c: Bandaging jewelry is unnecessary.
explanations.d: Skipping the AED is not appropriate.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.5 Recognize AED use with implanted devices, pregnancy, children 8 and older, and maintenance readiness
questions.text: A patient in arrest has an implanted pacemaker visible as a bulge in the upper-left chest. According to AHA Part 3, what is the correct AED pad placement?

answers.text: Place the pad directly over the pacemaker
Skip the AED entirely because of the pacemaker
Move the pacemaker first to a different location

Place the pad at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) away from the pacemaker — the device interferes with current delivery, and placing the pad over it can damage the device; standard anterior-lateral placement is usually compatible

explanations.a: A pad directly over the pacemaker reduces shock effectiveness and may damage the device.
explanations.b: Pacemakers are not a contraindication to AED use; just adjust pad placement.
explanations.c: Moving an implanted device is not possible during arrest.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3: place the pad ≥1 inch from a visible implanted device; this preserves shock effectiveness and protects the device.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.5 Recognize AED use with implanted devices, pregnancy, children 8 and older, and maintenance readiness
questions.keyword: pregnancy AED standard adult pads no modification
questions.text: A pregnant adult is in cardiac arrest. According to AHA Part 9 / Part 3, what AED considerations apply?

answers.text: Defibrillation is contraindicated during pregnancy
Use only pediatric pads regardless of patient size
Place pads on the abdomen instead of the chest

Use the AED with normal adult pad placement and standard energy — defibrillation is safe and effective during pregnancy and is performed for shockable rhythms; no modification to AED energy or placement is needed beyond standard CPR-in-pregnancy modifications (manual left uterine displacement)

explanations.a: Defibrillation is safe and indicated; pregnancy does not contraindicate AED use.
explanations.b: Pediatric pads on an adult deliver insufficient energy.
explanations.c: Abdominal placement does not target the heart.
explanations.d: AHA Part 9: defibrillation is safe in pregnancy; use standard adult pads, energy, and anterior-lateral placement; combine with manual left uterine displacement for CPR.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.5 Recognize AED use with implanted devices, pregnancy, children 8 and older, and maintenance readiness
questions.keyword: child 8 years older adult pads adult energy
questions.text: Per AHA Part 6 / Part 3, what is the correct AED approach for a child 8 years or older?

answers.text: Use only pediatric AED pads regardless of size
Skip the AED for children 8 and older
Reduce the energy manually before delivering a shock

Use adult AED pads and standard adult energy — children 8 and older (or weighing more than ~25 kg / 55 lbs) are treated with adult pads and standard energy; pediatric pads/attenuators are reserved for younger/smaller children

explanations.a: Pediatric pads are reserved for younger/smaller children; adult pads are appropriate for ≥8 years.
explanations.b: AED use is not skipped in children; just adjust pad selection.
explanations.c: AED energy is preprogrammed and not adjusted by rescuers.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 / Part 3: ≥8 years (or >25 kg) → adult pads + adult energy; <8 years (or <25 kg) → pediatric attenuator/pads if available, otherwise adult pads with anterior-posterior placement.

questions.name: AED Operation
questions.objective: 5.5 Recognize AED use with implanted devices, pregnancy, children 8 and older, and maintenance readiness
questions.keyword: AED maintenance battery pad expiration monthly check
questions.text: A workplace AED is found with a low-battery indicator and expired pads. According to AHA Part 3 / public-access defibrillation guidance, what is the correct response?

answers.text: Use the AED anyway in arrest; the battery may have enough charge for one shock
Discard the entire AED and order a replacement
Wait for arrest to occur before testing the AED

Replace the battery and pads immediately as part of routine maintenance — AHA recommends regular monthly checks (status indicator), battery replacement per manufacturer schedule, and pad replacement before expiration to ensure readiness when needed

explanations.a: Using a known-low battery during arrest is unreliable and could fail mid-shock.
explanations.b: Discarding the AED for routine maintenance is wasteful; replace consumables.
explanations.c: Reactive maintenance after arrest is too late.
explanations.d: AHA Part 3: AED maintenance includes regular checks (typically monthly), timely battery and pad replacement, and storage in a clearly marked, accessible location.
